critique.good: The team names wrap at word boundaries, while headers, numbers and signed goal differences stay intact. Consistent two-line rows make each record easy to follow, and the compact statistical columns keep related measures close together.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through GD and leaves Pts offscreen, so readers must scroll to see two measures central to the standings. The table is relatively tall because every team name wraps.
critique.cause: The 108px team column provides just enough room for the longest individual word but not for complete names. Together with the widths needed to keep the statistics intact, it makes the table 441px wide.

critique.good: More of the statistical columns appear in the initial viewport, and the table requires less horizontal scrolling than the other designs.
critique.problems: Team names, headers, numbers and signed differences split across lines. Uneven, tall rows make it difficult to identify teams and compare records, and Pts is still partly offscreen.
critique.cause: The 90px team column leaves only 69px for text, less than the longest team-name word. The 38px statistical columns leave 17px for text, which is too narrow for several values and headers.

critique.good: Every name and statistic stays on one line, producing compact, even rows and making each record easy to scan across.
critique.problems: The wide team column pushes most goal statistics and points beyond the initial viewport. Readers must scroll substantially to compare the measures most relevant to standings.
critique.cause: The 189px team column accommodates the longest full name, but contributes to a 522px table, 162px wider than the viewport.

critique.good: Team names and statistics are easy to scan, and the single two-line team name remains intact. The compact numeric columns keep the record readable.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through GA, leaving the rest of the goals group and points off-screen. Readers must scroll to see key standings information.
critique.cause: The 150px Team column and the minimum intact widths of the statistics columns produce a 483px table, 123px wider than the viewport.

critique.good: The team names have more breathing room, while the statistics and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: The extra width does not reduce the number of lines or improve row height. Less of the goals group is visible initially, and reaching points requires more scrolling.
critique.cause: Increasing Team from 150px to 170px adds 20px to the table without providing the 189px needed for the longest full name on one line.

critique.good: Team names wrap at spaces into consistent two-line rows, making each record easy to follow. Headers and signed goal differences stay intact, and the statistical columns have a regular rhythm.
critique.problems: Every team occupies two lines, yet the extra team-column space does not shorten any row. The initial viewport cuts into GD and leaves Pts offscreen, so readers must scroll to see two important standings measures.
critique.cause: The 120px team column provides 99px for text: enough to preserve individual words, but not enough to keep any full team name on one line. The total width is 453px.

critique.good: The 108px team column still preserves whole words and the same consistent two-line rows as r2A. Its narrower footprint brings more of GD into the initial viewport and reduces the scroll distance.
critique.problems: GD is still cut by the viewport edge and Pts is offscreen. All seven names still take two lines, creating a tall table for a short set of standings.
critique.cause: The team column provides 87px of text space, just enough for the longest unbreakable word. The statistical columns require a further 332px, giving a 441px rendered table.

r1A.idea: Widen the team column from r0A to allow shorter names to fit on one line while preserving intact words and statistics. This explores a middle ground between r0A's uniform wrapping and r0C's greater scrolling cost.

r1B.idea: Give team names more room while retaining the compact statistical columns. This tests whether a shorter table is worth the additional scrolling before committing to r0C's full one-line width.

r2A.idea: Reduce Team to 120px and D to its 32px content minimum. Individual words and numeric values remain intact; more team names may wrap, but more of the goals group fits initially and the table is 35px narrower than r1A.

r2B.idea: Use the 108px minimum that accommodates the longest team-name word, with all statistics intact. This tests the shortest scroll distance available without splitting words, at the cost of more wrapped team names.

r3A.idea: Widen Team to allow some shorter club names to fit on one line while preserving longer names at word boundaries. This may reduce table height, at the cost of moving more goal statistics beyond the initial viewport.

r3B.idea: Give Team its full 168px one-line content width plus padding. This tests a compact vertical layout with every club on one line, trading a substantially longer horizontal scroll for faster scanning down the team list.

understanding.purpose: Show league positions after 28 matches, supporting comparison of teams’ records, goal differences and points.
understanding.reading: Readers scan down the team names to find a club, then across its row to read its record; they also compare individual statistics down columns. Points and goal difference are especially relevant to standings.
groups: P, W, D and L describe matches played and results.
GF, GA and GD describe goals scored, conceded and the resulting difference.
Team identifies each row; Pts summarizes the points earned.
keep_intact: Numeric values, including the sign on goal differences.
Column headers and individual words in team names, where width permits.
may_wrap: Team names can wrap at spaces; their longer rows can absorb the extra line while the statistics remain aligned with the team.

bad.why: Team names, column headings and numeric values split within words or numbers. The resulting tall, irregular rows make standings difficult to scan, while the table still requires horizontal scrolling.

final.rationale: r1A keeps every heading and number intact, with only the longest team name wrapping, so most rows remain compact and easy to compare. Its initial viewport shows the team names and columns through GF, with GA beginning at the edge; GD and Pts require scrolling. The narrower two-line alternatives show more statistics initially but make every team row taller, while the wider designs gain little at first sight for the extra scrolling.

general: Keep numbers, signs and short column labels intact so readers can compare values reliably.
Allocate width according to content and column roles; consistent row rhythm and readable identifiers matter alongside total table width.
For a horizontally scrollable table, assess which columns are visible initially as well as the distance to the remaining columns.
specific: The team column benefits from enough width to keep most names on one line, while one natural wrap is a reasonable compromise.
The points column is important to the standings but lies outside the initial viewport in every candidate.

final.tradeoffs: r2B gives more statistical columns space in the initial viewport and reduces scrolling, at the cost of wrapping every team name and increasing table height. r0C and r3B keep every row on one line but require substantially more scrolling to reach points.
final.uncertain: The ranges are conservative judgments rather than browser-tested thresholds. Reasonable designers may prefer uniform two-line rows or prioritize seeing more statistics initially over compact team names.

A.why: Team names and visible figures remain intact, with only one name wrapping. The viewport reaches GF, but GA, GD and points require scrolling.

B.why: Fitting all columns into the viewport fragments team names, headers and numbers across many lines, making rows and comparisons very hard to read.

C.why: Names wrap at word boundaries and the figures remain intact. Most statistical columns are visible, though GD sits across the viewport edge and points require scrolling.

D.why: Team names, headers and figures split within words and numbers. The table still extends beyond the viewport, so the damage to readability does not eliminate scrolling.

E.why: Every team name stays on one line and the visible rows are easy to scan, but the wide team column leaves GF at the viewport edge and several statistics, including points, off-screen.

F.why: Names and figures stay intact, with only Harborough Wanderers wrapping. The viewport reaches GA, though that column straddles the edge and the remaining statistics require scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The screenshots do not show the full widths or contents of the columns beyond the right edge, so the total scrolling distance and the presentation of points cannot be assessed precisely.

A.why: Team names and visible figures stay on one line, but the wide team column leaves GF cut by the viewport and the remaining statistics require scrolling.

B.why: Only the longest team name wraps, while the visible figures remain intact. More statistics fit initially than in A, though GA is cut at the viewport edge and later columns require scrolling.

C.why: The table fits horizontally, but team names, headers and numbers split into fragments, making both row identification and comparison extremely difficult.

D.why: Team names wrap at word boundaries and figures remain intact. The compact team column brings most statistics into view, though GD is cut at the edge and points require scrolling.
